title: The lar–pileated gibbon contact zone: tension-zone clines with diffuse hybridization
content:
Abstract
Zones of contact and hybridization provide crucial opportunities for understanding the mechanisms that maintain species diversity and shape species boundaries. We investigated the spatial structure of the contact zone between lar gibbons and pileated gibbons in Khao Yai National Park, Thailand. Using a multi-species occupancy modelling framework, we analysed how the spatial distributions of the two gibbon species and their hybrids correlated geographical and environmental covariates. The two gibbon species showed strong west–east segregation in occupancy but also exhibited contrasting responses to elevation, stream density, and forest structure, suggesting that subtle habitat partitioning contributes to their coexistence within the zone. In contrast, hybrid and mixed-species groups, the forms that ultimately define the hybrid zone, showed weaker geographical and environmental structuring. Sigmoidal occupancy clines of the parental species are broadly consistent with a tension model, whereas the spatial distribution of hybrid and mixed-species groups does not conform to expectations of a narrow, centrally concentrated hybrid zone. Instead, the hybrid zone extends beyond a single central band and might encompass much of the park. Because the park is effectively isolated from surrounding parental populations, the gibbon hybrid zone might, over time, shift towards broader, more diffuse patterns of introgression.
